title: Algorithm Design and Analysis
subtitle: Choose an algorithm, trace its steps, prove its rule, and account for its cost.
description: Learn how to turn a problem into a correct and efficient algorithm. Begin with small stories and concrete inputs. Use Python to follow searching, sorting, graph traversal, greedy choices, divide and conquer, and randomization. Lists, trees, heaps and hash tables support the algorithms. Worked solutions explain why a method succeeds and when its assumptions fail.
coverage: Twenty-six connected topics cover correctness and cost, supporting data representations, graph algorithms, greedy proofs, divide and conquer, selection, randomization, and an introductory link to cryptographic complexity. This original learning guide explains mechanisms with small programs. It is not an official course or a collection of supplied assessment material. Production libraries and advanced cryptographic security proofs are outside its scope.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic: add, subtract, multiply and compare whole numbers. A logarithm counts repeated divisions; we explain it when needed.
Python basics: a variable gives a value a name; = assigns a value; == compares values. A list stores a sequence, and its first index is 0.
Control flow: an if statement chooses a branch; a for or while loop repeats work. Indentation groups the statements inside a branch, loop or function.
Functions: def names reusable steps; parameters are inputs; return sends a result back. A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem.
Objects: a class describes a record; self refers to one record; a field such as node.next stores data or a reference. None means no object is present.
Read a cost claim carefully: n counts items, O(n) means work has a linear upper bound for large n, and extra space counts storage beyond the input. Each topic explains its own assumptions.
outcomes: Specify the required answer and choose an algorithm that fits its assumptions
Trace state changes and use invariants or exchange arguments to explain correctness
Calculate worst-case, expected and amortized costs under an explicit cost model
Use lists, trees, heaps and hash tables to implement algorithmic choices
Distinguish shortest paths, spanning trees, sorting and selection objectives
Compare alternatives when data size, ordering, weights or available operations change

topics.title: Analyze growth and prove correctness
topics.story:
Mina packed lunch boxes for a school trip. After each new request, she added up the whole list again. Her friend kept a running total instead. Mina worried that the faster method might miss a request.

They wrote down a rule: after reading the first few requests, the running total must equal their sum. They checked the rule before the first request and after each addition. Both methods gave the same final total. The running method did much less repeated work. Mina now had two separate reasons to trust it: a rule explaining correctness and an operation count explaining speed.
topics.principle:
An algorithm is a sequence of steps. Its specification says what answer those steps must produce. First ask whether the answer is always correct. Then ask how much work the steps need. A fast wrong answer is still wrong.

Choose an input size n and count a clear operation, such as one addition. Big-O gives an upper growth bound. Big-Omega gives a lower bound. Big-Theta gives both. These are growth descriptions, not stopwatch times. Ordinary cost estimates assume the numbers fit in a machine word. Very large Python integers can cost more to process.

An invariant is a statement that stays true after every step. Show that it starts true, survives the next step, and gives the answer when the loop ends. Also explain why the loop ends. Worst-case cost means the hardest input of a given size. Expected cost averages over stated random choices. Amortized cost spreads expensive steps across a whole sequence; it does not require randomness.
topics.formula:
f(n) ∈ O(g(n)) ⇔ ∃c>0, n₀: 0≤f(n)≤cg(n) for all n≥n₀
1+2+⋯+n = n(n+1)/2
topics.symbols:
n counts input items. f(n) counts the chosen operation. g(n) is a simpler growth pattern used for comparison. The symbol ∈ means belongs to, and ⇔ means if and only if. The symbol ∃ means there exists.

c is a fixed positive multiplier. n₀ is a fixed starting size. For every n at least n₀, the cost must stay below c times g(n). The constants cannot change with n.

The sum 1+2+…+n counts loops with one step, then two, and so on. It equals n(n+1)/2 and grows as Θ(n²). Saying O(n³) is also true, but gives a less useful upper bound.
topics.example:
To compute prefix totals of [4,−1,6,2], keep a running sum s starting at zero. After reading each item, record s, producing [4,3,9,11]. The invariant is that after i iterations, s equals the sum of the first i input values and the first i outputs are correct.

It holds initially for i=0 and remains true when the next value is added. Four iterations give the whole answer. Computing each prefix from scratch would make 1+2+3+4=10 additions, while the running version uses four.

For length n the respective counts grow quadratically and linearly.
topics.pitfall: Calling O(n) an exact running time, or using an expected bound as though it were a worst-case guarantee.

check.question: If an algorithm is Θ(n), is it also O(n²)?
check.answer: Yes, for n≥1 a linear bound is also quadratic. Θ(n) is the more informative tight statement.

glossary.meaning: A statement that is true before and after every loop step.
The amount of data, often written n. State what you count.
The total cost of a sequence divided across its operations; no random choices are required.

guided_questions.question: Why is the running total initially correct?
guided_questions.answer: Before reading any values, the sum of the empty prefix is 0. The variable also starts at 0.

guided_questions.question: What happens when the third input, 6, arrives?
guided_questions.answer: The old total is 3. Adding 6 gives 9. This equals the sum of the first three values: 4 + (−1) + 6.

guided_questions.question: Does a single fast run prove a linear bound?
guided_questions.answer: No. A timing measures one situation. Counting one addition per input explains the linear bound for every input of that length.

code_examples.title: A running total and its invariant
code_examples.intro: A prefix is the part of a list from its beginning to some position. Print the total after every new value.
code_examples.code:
values = [4, -1, 6, 2]
total = 0
prefixes = []
for value in values:
    total += value
    prefixes.append(total)
    print(value, total)
print(prefixes)
code_examples.explanation:
values creates a Python list. total = 0 sets the initial sum. The empty brackets make an empty output list. The for loop gives value each input in order. += adds to the existing total; append places that total at the end.

The second printed column is always the sum seen so far. That is the invariant. Four inputs cause four additions. For n inputs, time is O(n), and storing every prefix needs O(n) extra space. Keeping only the final total would need O(1) extra variables under the fixed-size-number model.
walkthrough: Initialize total to the empty-prefix sum 0 and prefixes to an empty list.
Add the next value before recording total, preserving the processed-prefix invariant.
Print each transition and the complete prefix list after the loop.

code_examples.title: Count the cost of growing storage
code_examples.intro: Separate ordinary writes from copies caused by doubling capacity.
code_examples.code:
capacity = 1
size = 0
copies = 0
for value in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]:
    if size == capacity:
        copies += size
        capacity *= 2
    size += 1
    print("size:", size, "capacity:", capacity, "copies:", copies)
print("writes plus copies:", size + copies)
code_examples.output:
size: 1 capacity: 1 copies: 0
size: 2 capacity: 2 copies: 1
size: 3 capacity: 4 copies: 3
size: 4 capacity: 4 copies: 3
size: 5 capacity: 8 copies: 7
writes plus copies: 12
code_examples.explanation:
This is a cost simulation of a doubling array, not an implementation of Python list allocation. size counts occupied cells. When size equals capacity, every old reference would be copied, so copies increases by size before capacity doubles.

The fifth append causes four copies. It is expensive by itself. Across the five appends there are seven copies and five new writes. For n appends the geometric copy sum is below 2n, giving amortized O(1) append under this model. No random choices are involved.
walkthrough: Start with one available cell and no stored values.
Before each write, double only if every current cell is occupied.
Charge each old cell once for a resize, then charge one new write.

instructor_notes.title: A proof and a count answer different questions
instructor_notes.body: The prefix invariant proves every recorded sum is correct, including inputs with negative values. Counting one addition per item proves linear arithmetic work. Neither a plausible output nor a fast timing supplies both arguments.

instructor_notes.title: One costly operation can fit a cheap sequence
instructor_notes.body: For doubling storage, copied blocks have sizes 1, 2, 4 and so on. Their geometric sum stays proportional to the final capacity. This is an amortized argument, unlike the expected search bound in the skip-list chapter, which depends on random towers.

worked_problems.title: Cost of all prefixes
worked_problems.question: For n=8 values, compare recomputing each prefix with maintaining one running sum. Count additions starting from zero.
worked_problems.strategy: Count how often each loop performs an addition; do not infer complexity from timing.
steps: Recomputing prefixes costs 1+2+…+8 additions.
Use 8×9/2=36 to evaluate this arithmetic series.
A running total reads each of 8 values once, so it uses 8 additions.
worked_problems.answer: The running method saves 28 additions and is Θ(n), versus Θ(n²) for recomputation.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Both produce the same eight outputs by the prefix invariant. For n=0, both do zero additions.

topics.title: Arrays, linked lists and ADT contracts
topics.story:
Ravi kept reading cards in numbered boxes. Finding box 4 was easy. Inserting a new card near the beginning meant moving many later cards. He tried a second design: each card held a link to the next card.

Now he could insert a card by changing links. But he still had to follow the chain to find the insertion place. Ravi used numbered boxes for frequent indexed reads. He used linked cards when he already had a reference to the position being edited. He learned to count the search and the edit separately.
topics.principle:
A list is an ordered collection. An abstract data type, or ADT, states allowed operations without choosing storage. For example, a list may promise to read item i or insert before item i. Its contract must also say what happens for an invalid position.

An array stores equal-sized cells in a row. Its address formula lets us reach cell i directly. A Python list uses a resizable array of references. Reading an index is O(1). Inserting in the middle shifts later references and can take O(n). An occasional resize makes one append expensive, although append is amortized O(1).

A linked list stores separate nodes. Each node holds a value and a next reference. A doubly linked node also remembers its previous node. Changing a fixed number of links at an already known position is O(1). Finding index i still needs a walk. A singly linked deletion usually needs the previous node; knowing only the node to remove is not enough under the usual node-identity contract. A sentinel is a dummy endpoint that simplifies edge cases.
topics.formula:
Array address(i) = base + i·cell_size
Array indexed access: O(1)
Linked-list indexed access: O(n); local doubly linked edit: O(1)
topics.symbols:
i is an index, starting at 0. base is the address of the first array cell. cell_size is the fixed width of a cell. Multiplying i by cell_size gives its distance from the beginning.

n is the number of stored items. O(1) means the number of basic steps does not grow with n. O(n) allows a number of steps proportional to n. A constant-time linked edit assumes the required node references are already known. Include the cost of finding them. Python list cells hold references; the objects themselves need not sit next to each other.
topics.example:
Store [L,M,N,P] in an array. Inserting X at index 1 shifts M, N and P one position right, then writes X, yielding [L,X,M,N,P]. In a doubly linked representation with a direct reference to M, let left=M.prev and create X.

Set X.prev=left, X.next=M, left.next=X and M.prev=X. Only a fixed number of links change. But if the request arrives merely as “insert at index 1,” the list must first find that position; for a general index near the far end, that traversal can dominate.

The contract must also reject invalid positions or define their behavior.
topics.pitfall: Saying all linked-list operations are O(1). Only certain operations at already located positions have that bound.

check.question: Which representation is a natural fit for millions of random indexed reads and rare middle insertions?
check.answer: An array-based list, because direct indexing is constant time and its occasional shifting cost may be acceptable.

glossary.meaning: An abstract data type: a promise about operations and results, separate from its implementation.
A small record containing a value and references to other nodes.
A way to reach an existing object. Assigning a reference does not copy the whole object.

guided_questions.question: Why does inserting at array index 1 shift three items here?
guided_questions.answer: In [L, M, N, P], M, N and P must each move one position to leave room for X.

guided_questions.question: Why save old_next before changing m.next?
guided_questions.answer: It keeps access to the rest of the chain. Without that reference, replacing the link could disconnect later nodes.

guided_questions.question: Is a linked-list insertion always O(1)?
guided_questions.answer: Only the link change at a known place is O(1). Walking to that place may take O(n).

code_examples.title: See an array insertion shift values
code_examples.intro: Build an insertion by hand instead of hiding it inside list.insert.
code_examples.code:
items = ["L", "M", "N", "P"]
position = 1
items.append(None)
shifts = 0
for i in range(len(items) - 1, position, -1):
    items[i] = items[i - 1]
    shifts += 1
items[position] = "X"
print(items)
print("shifts:", shifts)
code_examples.explanation:
append(None) creates one spare cell. None is a placeholder, not the text "None". range(start, stop, -1) visits indices backward and excludes stop. Moving backward avoids overwriting a value before copying it.

The loop moves P, then N, then M. The final assignment writes X into index 1. The output counts three shifted references. In the worst case, n existing items move, so insertion is O(n). This example grows a Python list; it does not expose physical memory addresses.
walkthrough: Append a spare cell so the last item has a destination.
Copy entries from right to left, preserving values not copied yet.
Fill the gap at position 1 with X and report three shifts.

code_examples.title: Insert a real node into a linked chain
code_examples.intro: Here the program already knows node M. Watch it insert X after M without moving N.
code_examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next_node=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next_node

n = Node("N")
m = Node("M", n)
head = Node("L", m)
old_next = m.next
m.next = Node("X", old_next)
values = []
current = head
while current is not None:
    values.append(current.value)
    current = current.next
print(values)
print("X still links to N:", m.next.next is n)
code_examples.output:
['L', 'M', 'X', 'N']
X still links to N: True
code_examples.explanation:
class defines the shape of a node. __init__ runs when Node(...) creates one. self names that new node. The next field holds a reference, and None marks the end. Constructing N first lets M point to N and L point to M.

old_next remembers N. The new X points to N, and M now points to X. The is test asks whether two references reach the very same object. The edit uses constant work. The printing walk uses O(n) time and an O(n) result list; that display cost is separate from insertion.
walkthrough: Construct the chain backward so every next reference already exists.
Save M’s successor, create X pointing to it, then redirect M to X.
Follow next references and check that the old N object remains linked.

instructor_notes.title: Choose the representation from the operation
instructor_notes.body: A list contract does not promise a particular cost. If an algorithm repeatedly reads index i, an array gives direct access. If it already holds both neighboring node references, linked splicing avoids shifting a suffix. Counting only the edit can hide the search that found its location.

instructor_notes.title: Preserve access before replacing links
instructor_notes.body: Saving old_next keeps the suffix reachable while M receives a new next link. This is an ownership-style invariant: every original node remains reachable exactly once in the final chain. A cyclic link would make the simple display loop fail to terminate.

worked_problems.title: Search before editing
worked_problems.question: A 100-node singly linked list is indexed from 0. Insert before index 80 using only its head. Compare with an array of 100 items.
worked_problems.strategy: Separate locating the predecessor from changing links, then count the array suffix.
steps: The linked predecessor is index 79, reached by 79 next-link moves from index 0.
Create one node and reconnect the predecessor and old successor using constant work.
The array shifts indices 80 through 99: 100−80=20 references.
worked_problems.answer: Both requests can have linear cost; the linked edit alone is constant only after its predecessor is known.
worked_problems.sanity_check: If a predecessor reference is supplied directly, the 79-link search disappears.

topics.title: Stacks, queues and circular storage
topics.story:
Noor ran a school print desk. She first kept incoming jobs in a pile and always took the top sheet. New arrivals kept delaying the oldest job. She changed to a waiting line, with new jobs at one end and service at the other. Everyone was then served in arrival order.

Later, she added an undo button to the editing program. This time the most recent action had to be removed first, so the pile rule was correct. Noor learned that the right structure depends on which item should leave next, not on how many items it stores.
topics.principle:
A stack removes the newest item first. This is last in, first out, or LIFO. push adds an item; pop removes the top. A stack fits undo history and nested brackets. A queue removes the oldest item first. This is first in, first out, or FIFO. enqueue adds at the back; dequeue removes at the front.

A Python list works well as a stack with append and pop at its end. For a queue, collections.deque supports efficient operations at both ends. Using list.pop(0) shifts the remaining items and takes O(n).

A circular queue reuses a fixed array. It stores a front index and a size. Modulo wraps an index to the beginning. The size distinguishes full from empty. Reject an enqueue when full, or define a resize rule. Never dequeue an empty queue. For bracket checking, each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket.
topics.formula:
Queue insertion index = (front + size) mod capacity
After dequeue: front ← (front+1) mod capacity; size ← size−1
topics.symbols:
front is the index of the oldest queued item. size counts current items. capacity is the number of physical slots and must be positive. mod is the remainder after division; Python writes it as %.

The insertion index is front plus size, wrapped into the slot range. After removing one item, advance front by one with the same wrap and reduce size by one. The arrow ← means replace the old value. These rules change storage positions but preserve FIFO order. Fixed-capacity updates use O(1) work.
topics.example:
Use a capacity-five queue with front=3 and size=3. Its items A, B and C occupy indices 3, 4 and 0. Enqueue D at (3+3) mod 5=1, raising size to four.

Dequeue returns A, advances front to 4 and reduces size to three. The logical order is now B,C,D even though the occupied physical slots wrap across the array boundary. No items are shifted.

As a separate stack trace, the string ([ ]) with spaces ignored pushes ( then [, pops [ on ], and pops ( on ); the final empty stack confirms proper nesting.
topics.pitfall: Using a queue to validate nesting, or shifting an entire array on every dequeue when a circular index scheme would suffice.

check.question: Why does the bracket string ([)] fail despite equal counts of openers and closers?
check.answer: The first closer ) does not match the current stack top [. Correct nesting requires matching the most recent unmatched opener.

glossary.meaning: Last in, first out: the newest stored item leaves first.
First in, first out: the oldest stored item leaves first.
The remainder after division. It wraps an index into a fixed range.

guided_questions.question: Why does a stack reject ([)]?
guided_questions.answer: When ) arrives, [ is still on top. Counts alone cannot detect this wrong nesting order.

guided_questions.question: What does deque.popleft remove?
guided_questions.answer: It removes the leftmost item. If new items were appended on the right, this is the oldest item.

guided_questions.question: Why keep size in a circular queue?
guided_questions.answer: The same front and back positions can occur when a ring is empty or full. A size value makes the state clear.

code_examples.title: Match brackets with a stack
code_examples.intro: The function checks both matching types and matching order.
code_examples.explanation:
def creates a reusable function. opening maps each closing bracket to its required opening bracket. append records an opening bracket. not stack is true for an empty stack; or stops immediately in that case, so pop is safe.

A closer removes only the top opening bracket. A mismatch returns False immediately. At the end, not stack rejects leftover openings. Other characters are ignored. Each character is examined once, giving O(n) time. At most n opening brackets are stored, giving O(n) extra space.
walkthrough: Map each closer to its opener and begin with no unmatched brackets.
Push openers; a closer must safely pop a matching top.
Reject early mismatches and reject leftover openers after the scan.

code_examples.title: Serve waiting jobs with deque
code_examples.intro: A deque is a double-ended queue. Use its right end for arrival and left end for service.
code_examples.code:
from collections import deque
queue = deque(["Ada", "Bo"])
queue.append("Cy")
print("served:", queue.popleft())
print("waiting:", list(queue))
queue.appendleft("urgent")
print("left end:", queue.popleft())
print("waiting:", list(queue))
code_examples.output:
served: Ada
waiting: ['Bo', 'Cy']
left end: urgent
waiting: ['Bo', 'Cy']
code_examples.explanation:
The import makes deque available. append adds Cy on the right. popleft removes Ada, who arrived first. list(queue) makes a list only so the state prints clearly.

appendleft shows a different operation: it places urgent ahead of the waiting jobs. This changes the service policy, so that part is no longer pure FIFO. Deque endpoint additions and removals take O(1) time. Copying all waiting items for display takes O(n). An empty popleft would raise IndexError.
walkthrough: Append Cy behind Ada and Bo, preserving arrival order.
Remove Ada from the left and display the two remaining jobs.
Insert urgent at the left to demonstrate an explicit change of policy.

instructor_notes.title: The removal rule is part of the algorithm
instructor_notes.body: Bracket matching needs the newest unmatched opening bracket, so a stack is essential to its proof. BFS needs the oldest waiting vertex, so a queue preserves distance layers. Replacing either container without changing the proof can silently change the algorithm.

instructor_notes.title: Wrap positions, not the logical order
instructor_notes.body: In a ring, indices may decrease when they wrap, but arrival order must not change. Keeping size prevents full and empty from having an ambiguous representation. The fixed-capacity O(1) bound excludes resizing and copying a whole queue for display.

worked_problems.title: Wrap without shifting
worked_problems.question: A ring has capacity 5, front 3 and items A,B,C at slots 3,4,0. Enqueue D, then dequeue once.
worked_problems.strategy: Track logical size separately from physical indices.
steps: Initially size=3; the insertion index is (3+3)%5=1.
Store D at 1 and set size=4. Logical order is A,B,C,D.
Remove A; front becomes (3+1)%5=4 and size becomes 3.
worked_problems.answer: The remaining order is B,C,D at slots 4,0,1. No existing item shifts.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Walking size=3 positions from front=4 modulo 5 visits exactly 4,0,1.

topics.title: Tree structure and traversal order
topics.story:
Lena made a directory of props for a school play. One box contained costumes and tools. The costume box contained hats and coats. She wanted one list for opening boxes and another for packing them away.

For opening, Lena wrote the parent box before its contents. For packing, she finished every smaller box before closing its parent. Both lists included every item, but their order served different jobs. She also counted each box by adding the counts reported by its children. The directory became easier to process when she treated each smaller branch as the same kind of problem.
topics.principle:
A tree connects nodes without cycles. A rooted tree chooses one node as its starting point. Every other node has one parent. A child belongs directly below a parent. A leaf has no children. In a binary tree, each node has at most a left child and a right child.

Preorder visits the node before its children. Postorder visits the children first. Inorder, for a binary tree, visits the left branch, the node, then the right branch. Inorder is sorted only when the tree also satisfies the binary-search-tree rule.

Recursion means asking the same function to handle a smaller branch. The empty branch is the stopping case. Computing child results once and combining them gives O(n) traversal time. Active function calls need O(h) extra space, where h is tree height. A chain can have height n−1. Python limits recursion depth, so very deep trees may need an explicit stack. An Euler tour describes the first, middle and final visits around each binary node; these give the three traversal orders.
topics.formula:
size(v) = 1 + Σu child of v size(u)
height(v) = 1 + maxu child of v height(u)
Leaf height = 0
topics.symbols:
v names a node. u ranges over its children, and Σ means add their results. size(v) counts v and all nodes below it. Add 1 for v itself.

Height counts edges, not nodes. A leaf has height 0. For a nonleaf, take the largest child height and add 1. A binary implementation can give an empty branch height −1, so the same rule also works for leaves. n is total nodes; h is root height. Keep this convention consistent.
topics.example:
Let root R have children A and B. Let A have children C and D, and B have one child E. Preorder is R,A,C,D,B,E; postorder is C,D,A,E,B,R.

In postorder, C,D and E each report size one. A combines its children to obtain three, B obtains two, and R obtains six. Heights are zero for the leaves, one for A and B, and two for R.

The recursion computes each result once. An algorithm that recomputes every subtree size separately at each ancestor could waste quadratic work on a chain, despite using the same recurrence conceptually.
topics.pitfall: Assuming every binary tree is balanced. “Binary” limits children per node; it does not bound height logarithmically.

check.question: Which traversal naturally deletes an entire tree when children must be removed before their parent?
check.answer: Postorder, because each subtree is processed before the node that owns it.

glossary.meaning: The chosen starting node of a tree.
One node together with all nodes below it.
A function calling itself on a smaller problem until it reaches a stopping case.

guided_questions.question: Why does postorder help compute size?
guided_questions.answer: A parent needs its child sizes first. Postorder completes those calculations before combining them.

guided_questions.question: What is the height of a single-node tree?
guided_questions.answer: It is 0 under the edge-count convention. There is no downward edge to travel.

guided_questions.question: Is inorder always sorted?
guided_questions.answer: No. It follows a structural order. Sorted output also requires the binary-search-tree key invariant.

code_examples.title: Compare three traversal orders
code_examples.intro: Represent a node as a tuple containing its label, left branch and right branch. None is an empty branch.
code_examples.explanation:
A tuple groups three values. The assignment value, left, right unpacks them. The None case returns an empty list and stops recursion. The two recursive calls handle smaller branches. The + signs join lists in the requested order.

Every node appears once in each output. However, repeated list joining copies results. This clear teaching version can take O(n²) time on a chain and need O(n) peak temporary list storage in addition to the O(h) call stack. A production traversal can append to one result list for O(n) time and O(n) output plus O(h) call-stack space.
walkthrough: Return an empty sequence for None, the stopping case.
Recursively obtain left and right orders, then place the current label before, between or after them.
Run the same tree through all three placement rules.

code_examples.title: Calculate size and height together
code_examples.intro: Return both facts from each branch so no branch needs a second scan.
code_examples.code:
tree = ("R", ("A", ("C", None, None), None), ("B", None, None))
def facts(node):
    if node is None:
        return 0, -1
    _, left, right = node
    left_size, left_height = facts(left)
    right_size, right_height = facts(right)
    return 1 + left_size + right_size, 1 + max(left_height, right_height)

size, height = facts(tree)
print("size:", size)
print("height:", height)
print("empty:", facts(None))
code_examples.explanation:
The empty branch returns size 0 and height −1. The underscore means the label is deliberately unused. Each recursive call returns a pair, which the next assignment unpacks. The parent adds sizes and takes the larger height.

The root counts four nodes. The longest route R–A–C uses two edges, so height is 2. Each node does constant combining work once: O(n) time. Only the active ancestor calls need storage, so extra space is O(h). These small trees stay safely below Python's recursion limit.
walkthrough: Use (0,-1) for an empty branch to make the formulas work at leaves.
Request size and height together from each child.
Add one for the parent and choose the longer child height.

instructor_notes.title: Compute each child result once
instructor_notes.body: The size-height routine returns two facts together. Recomputing every descendant size at every ancestor would revisit a chain quadratically often. This connects to dynamic programming: retain an already solved subproblem instead of repeating it.

instructor_notes.title: Output construction also costs time
instructor_notes.body: The three-order example joins lists for clarity. Joining copies entries, so visiting each node once does not by itself prove linear total time. Appending to one shared output list removes that repeated copying while keeping the traversal rule unchanged.

worked_problems.title: Combine subtree facts
worked_problems.question: Root R has children A and B. A has leaves C and D; B has leaf E. Count nodes and edge-height.
worked_problems.strategy: Work from leaves upward so every child result is already available.
steps: Each leaf has size 1 and height 0.
A has size 1+1+1=3 and height 1; B has size 1+1=2 and height 1.
R has size 1+3+2=6 and height 1+max(1,1)=2.
worked_problems.answer: There are six nodes and a longest downward path of two edges.
worked_problems.sanity_check: List R,A,B,C,D,E to independently count six; R→A→C has two edges.

topics.title: Binary search trees and output-sensitive queries
topics.story:
Omar stored numbered library tags in a tree. At each tag, lower numbers went left and higher numbers went right. Finding tag 22 no longer required checking every tag. He compared with 18, turned right at 27, then found 22 on its left.

A teacher later requested every tag from 10 to 28. Omar skipped branches that were entirely too small or too large. When he removed the root tag, he used the next larger tag as its replacement. The tree stayed searchable because he preserved the ordering of whole branches, not just neighboring nodes.
topics.principle:
A binary search tree, or BST, gives each node a key. Every key in its left subtree must be smaller. Every key in its right subtree must be larger. The rule applies to all descendants. In these examples, inserting an existing key leaves one copy. A map could instead replace that key's value.

Search compares the target with the current key and chooses one branch. Insertion follows that route until it reaches an empty position. Delete a leaf directly. For one child, connect the parent to that child. For two children, use the smallest key in the right subtree, called the successor, then remove its old node.

Search and updates take O(h), where h is height. A balanced tree has logarithmic height; a badly shaped tree can be a chain. A range query visits useful branches and outputs keys between two bounds. Its O(h+k) cost includes writing k answers. This is output-sensitive: a large answer necessarily costs more.
topics.formula:
∀u in left(v), key(u)<key(v); ∀w in right(v), key(v)<key(w)
Search/update: O(h); report range: O(h+k)
topics.symbols:
v is the node whose key we compare. u and w name any nodes in its left and right subtrees. key reads a stored key. ∀ means for every, so the rule is about whole subtrees.

h is tree height, n is the number of nodes, and k is the number of reported keys. The query includes both endpoints of [a,b]. Even a perfect search cannot write k answers in fewer than Ω(k) output steps. O(log n) requires a balancing rule; an ordinary BST does not guarantee it.
topics.example:
Insert keys 18, 9, 27, 4, 13, 22 and 31 into an empty BST. Searching for 22 visits 18,27,22. A query for [10,28] reports 13,18,22,27 in order, pruning the subtree rooted at 4 and excluding 31 from the output.

To delete 18, choose its inorder successor 22, the smallest key in the right subtree. Move the entry 22 into the root position and remove its old node, which has no left child. The resulting tree keeps the ordering invariant.

Merely replacing the root with an arbitrary descendant, such as 31, would violate the placement of smaller keys in the right subtree.
topics.pitfall: Checking only that a left child is smaller and a right child larger. The ordering restriction applies to entire subtrees.

check.question: What happens if increasing keys are inserted into an ordinary empty BST?
check.answer: They form a rightward chain, giving linear height and linear worst-case lookup despite the BST ordering invariant.

glossary.meaning: The value used to order and find a record.
The next larger key; for a node with a right branch, its smallest key lies down that branch's leftmost path.
A cost bound that includes the number of answers produced.

guided_questions.question: Why can search skip the left branch after seeing 18 when looking for 22?
guided_questions.answer: Every key in that left branch is smaller than 18. None can be 22.

guided_questions.question: What does a query for [10,28] return here?
guided_questions.answer: It returns 13, 18, 22 and 27. Both query endpoints are included if they are stored.

guided_questions.question: What happens if increasing keys are inserted without balancing?
guided_questions.answer: They form a rightward chain. Search may inspect every node, so its worst-case cost becomes O(n).

code_examples.title: Insert keys and record the search route
code_examples.intro: These are actual linked tree nodes, not a call to Python sorting.
code_examples.explanation:
Each Node starts with two empty child references. insert returns the root of the updated branch. Assigning its result to node.left or node.right keeps the new child connected. Equal keys take neither branch, so this example stores unique keys.

The while loop records each comparison. The conditional expression chooses left when the target is smaller, otherwise right. It reaches 22 after three visits. Search takes O(h) time and O(1) working references; route uses O(h) display space. Recursive insertion uses O(h) stack space and does not balance the tree.
walkthrough: Insert each key by reconnecting the root returned by the recursive call.
At each comparison, rule out the subtree on the wrong side.
Stop at 22 or at None, recording the route for inspection.

code_examples.title: Report a range without visiting every branch
code_examples.intro: Use a nested tuple to keep this range-query example short. Each tuple is key, left, right.
code_examples.explanation:
The function shares one result list across calls. It enters the left subtree only when smaller keys might still reach low. It appends the current key only if both bounds accept it. It enters the right subtree only when larger keys might still fit below high.

These three actions follow inorder order, so the printed answer is sorted. The tests skip the branch rooted at 4. They visit 31 but exclude it from the output and do not enter its right subtree. With unique keys and a valid BST, time is O(h+k). Output needs O(k) storage, and recursive calls need O(h). The example assumes low is no greater than high.
walkthrough: Check whether the left subtree could intersect the lower bound.
Append the current key only when both inclusive bounds accept it.
Check the right subtree separately to retain inorder output.

instructor_notes.title: Pruning needs a global ordering rule
instructor_notes.body: If a node key is below the query’s lower bound, every key in its left subtree is also too small. That conclusion uses the rule for all descendants, not only the left child. A locally plausible but invalid BST can make pruning omit a valid answer.

instructor_notes.title: Output size is an unavoidable cost
instructor_notes.body: Even a perfectly balanced tree cannot list n matching keys in O(log n) time. O(h+k) separates the boundary search from writing k answers. A count-only query could use stored subtree sizes, but that is a different operation with extra metadata to maintain.

worked_problems.title: A range with necessary output work
worked_problems.question: Use the BST with insertion order 18,9,27,4,13,22,31. Report keys in [10,28].
worked_problems.strategy: Use subtree ordering to prune and inorder to keep answers sorted.
steps: At 9, the entire left subtree is below 10, so skip key 4. Visit 13.
Root 18 is in range. In its right subtree, 22 and 27 are also in range.
Key 31 is above 28, so report only 13,18,22,27. Here k=4 and h=2.
worked_problems.answer: Four ordered keys are returned. The O(h+k) bound includes the unavoidable four output entries.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A full inorder list is [4,9,13,18,22,27,31]; filtering it gives the same answer.

topics.title: AVL balance and local rotations
topics.story:
Tess inserted shelf numbers 30, 20 and 10 into a search tree. Each number went left, leaving a long chain. Her search tree was correct, but it was starting to behave like a slow list.

She moved 20 to the top of this small branch. It kept 10 on the left and placed 30 on the right. Reading from left to right still gave 10, 20, 30. The routes were now shorter. Tess then tried 30, 10, 20 and needed two small rotations. She learned that balance repairs change links while preserving the order of keys.
topics.principle:
An AVL tree is a BST with one extra rule. At every node, the left and right child heights may differ by at most one. Height measures the longest downward route. Store a height at each node so it can be updated from its children.

After inserting or deleting with BST rules, walk back toward the root. A rotation reconnects a few nearby nodes. One rotation repairs an outer-heavy shape. An inner-heavy shape needs a rotation at the child followed by a rotation at the parent. Always update the lower node's height before the new root's height. Inorder key order stays unchanged.

The fewest nodes possible at height h obey a Fibonacci-like recurrence. This forces height O(log n), giving worst-case logarithmic search and updates. Deletion can reduce several ancestor heights. It may need more repairs after the first rotation. The examples below demonstrate rotations; they are not a complete AVL insertion or deletion library.
topics.formula:
|height(left(v))−height(right(v))| ≤ 1
N(h)=1+N(h−1)+N(h−2), N(−1)=0, N(0)=1
topics.symbols:
height(left(v)) and height(right(v)) are the heights of node v's child branches. The vertical bars around their difference mean absolute value: ignore its sign. An empty branch has height −1; a leaf has height 0.

N(h) is the smallest node count for an AVL tree of height h. One child must have height h−1, and the smallest allowed other child has height h−2. Add 1 for the root. N(−1)=0 and N(0)=1 start the recurrence. The quickly growing node count prevents a tall tree with very few nodes.
topics.example:
Insert 30,20,10 into an initially empty AVL tree. Before repair, 30 has a left child 20, which has a left child 10. Node 30 has child heights one and −1, a difference of two.

Rotate right at 30: 20 becomes the subtree root, 10 its left child and 30 its right child. Inorder remains 10,20,30, so the BST property is unchanged, while all balance differences become zero. For insertion order 30,10,20, the heavy path bends inward.

Rotate left at 10 first, then right at 30; the same balanced result is obtained through a double rotation.
topics.pitfall: Rebalancing from stale heights, or assuming one rotation is enough for every case. Identify the child and grandchild directions and update metadata consistently.

check.question: Does a rotation change the sorted order returned by inorder traversal?
check.answer: No. A correct rotation rearranges parent relationships while preserving the relative inorder sequence of all keys and attached subtrees.

glossary.meaning: Left-child height minus right-child height. AVL permits −1, 0 or 1.
A local change of child links that preserves the inorder sequence.
Extra stored facts about a node, such as its height.

guided_questions.question: Why is 30 unbalanced before rotating 30–20–10?
guided_questions.answer: Its left child has height 1 and its missing right child has height −1. Their difference is 2.

guided_questions.question: Why update the old root before the new root?
guided_questions.answer: The new root's height depends on the repaired old root. Using the old height could store a wrong result.

guided_questions.question: Does one successful rotation finish every AVL deletion?
guided_questions.answer: No. The repaired branch can become shorter, making another ancestor unbalanced. Continue checking upward.

code_examples.title: Rotate an outer-heavy branch right
code_examples.intro: All nodes store heights. The helper recalculates a node after its links change.
code_examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key):
        self.key, self.left, self.right, self.height = key, None, None, 0
def height(node):
    return -1 if node is None else node.height
def update(node):
    node.height = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))
def rotate_right(root):
    new_root = root.left
    root.left = new_root.right
    new_root.right = root
    update(root)
    update(new_root)
    return new_root
root = Node(30)
root.left = Node(20)
root.left.left = Node(10)
update(root.left)
update(root)
print("before height:", root.height)
root = rotate_right(root)
print("keys:", root.left.key, root.key, root.right.key)
print("after height:", root.height)
code_examples.explanation:
The class stores each key, two links and a height. height(None) supplies the empty-branch convention. update uses stored child heights. rotate_right first saves the left child. It moves that child's old right branch to the old root's left, then makes the old root its right child.

Updating the old root first makes the new root's height calculation valid. The printed keys show the same sorted order; height falls from 2 to 1. Each rotation uses O(1) time and space with stored heights. Finding the repair point still takes O(h). This function assumes the left child exists.
walkthrough: Build 30→20→10 and update heights from the leaf upward.
Promote the left child while transferring its middle subtree to the old root.
Update the old root before the promoted root, then inspect height and order.

code_examples.title: Repair an inner-heavy branch
code_examples.intro: First straighten 30–10–20 with a left rotation. Then perform a right rotation.
code_examples.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key, left=None, right=None):
        self.key, self.left, self.right = key, left, right
def rotate_left(root):
    top = root.right
    root.right = top.left
    top.left = root
    return top
def rotate_right(root):
    top = root.left
    root.left = top.right
    top.right = root
    return top
root = Node(30, Node(10, right=Node(20)))
root.left = rotate_left(root.left)
print("after first:", root.key, root.left.key, root.left.left.key)
root = rotate_right(root)
print("after second:", root.left.key, root.key, root.right.key)
code_examples.explanation:
The first tree bends left and then right. rotate_left promotes 20 above 10, converting the bend into a leftward chain. The assignment to root.left reconnects that changed branch. rotate_right then promotes 20 above 30.

The final print uses left, root, right order and shows 10, 20, 30. These link changes cost O(1). To focus on the two shapes, this second example omits height fields; a full AVL implementation must update metadata after both rotations, as the first example does. Neither function handles a missing required child.
walkthrough: Recognize the left-right bend before choosing a repair.
Rotate at child 10 and reconnect the returned root 20 to node 30.
Rotate at 30 to make 20 the root and inspect both children.

instructor_notes.title: Rotations preserve more than three keys
instructor_notes.body: In a right rotation, the promoted child’s right subtree moves to the old root’s left. Its keys lie between those two roots, so this transfer preserves all BST inequalities. Dropping that middle subtree would lose data even if the printed root keys look sorted.

instructor_notes.title: Metadata determines the next repair
instructor_notes.body: Update heights from the bottom upward because a parent depends on its new child heights. After deletion, a repaired branch may be shorter and trigger another repair above. The single-rotation demonstrations do not replace the full upward maintenance algorithm.

worked_problems.title: How few nodes can a tall AVL tree contain?
worked_problems.question: Use N(−1)=0, N(0)=1 and N(h)=1+N(h−1)+N(h−2). Find N(3) and N(4).
worked_problems.strategy: Compute smaller heights first and use the least-balanced allowed children.
steps: N(4)=1+7+4=12. Each child-height gap is at most one.
worked_problems.answer: An AVL tree of height 4 needs at least 12 nodes; 11 nodes cannot support that height.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A perfect height-4 binary tree has 31 nodes, which exceeds the minimum as expected.

topics.title: Priority queues and binary heaps
topics.story:
A robotics club shared one printer. Jules assigned each print job a priority number; smaller numbers meant greater urgency. Sorting the whole waiting list after every arrival felt wasteful. He only needed the smallest number next.

Jules arranged the jobs so each parent had no larger priority than its children. The smallest was always at the top. A new urgent job moved upward until the rule held again. After removing the top job, he moved the final job there and repaired downward. The rest of the jobs were not fully sorted, but the next urgent job was always easy to find.
topics.principle:
A priority queue returns the item with the best priority. A min-heap uses the smallest key as best. It keeps two rules: parents are no larger than children, and the tree fills each level from left to right. This complete shape fits naturally into an array.

Insertion appends a key at the end. Compare it with its parent and swap while it is smaller. Removal saves the root, puts the last key at the root, then swaps downward with the smaller child until the rule holds. The height is logarithmic, so each repair takes O(log n). Reading the minimum is O(1).

Building a heap from the bottom up is O(n), because most nodes are near the leaves. Repeated insertion has an O(n log n) upper bound. Python's heapq works directly on a list. Equal priorities do not automatically give arrival order; add a sequence number if that matters. A heap array is not a sorted array.
topics.formula:
parent(i)=⌊(i−1)/2⌋; left(i)=2i+1; right(i)=2i+2
A[parent(i)] ≤ A[i] for i>0
topics.symbols:
A is the heap array. i is a zero-based index. The floor signs ⌊ ⌋ mean round down; Python's // performs integer division for these nonnegative indices. For a nonroot node, (i−1)//2 gives its parent.

The child indices are 2i+1 and 2i+2. A child exists only if its index is below the current length n. The parent inequality applies when i>0. It guarantees a minimum at index 0, but says nothing about the relative order of two siblings.
topics.example:
Begin with min-heap array [3,8,5,12,10]. Insert 4 at index 5, whose parent is index 2 holding 5. Swap those entries to obtain [3,8,4,12,10,5]; 4 is now below 3, so stop.

Remove the minimum 3 by placing the final 5 at the root and reducing size: [5,8,4,12,10]. Compare children 8 and 4, swap with the smaller child 4, and finish at [4,8,5,12,10]. The removed value was correct because heap order puts a minimum at the root.

Notice that 8 precedes 5 in the array; a heap is not a sorted list.
topics.pitfall: Using a heap as though it supported arbitrary-key search in O(log n). Without an auxiliary index, locating an arbitrary key can require O(n).

check.question: Why swap a sinking element with the smaller child in a min-heap?
check.answer: Using the larger child could leave that parent larger than its other child, violating heap order immediately.

glossary.meaning: A collection that removes an item according to priority rather than arrival time.
Every parent key is no larger than either child key.
A binary tree whose levels fill from left to right without gaps.

guided_questions.question: Why can index 0 hold a minimum without sorting all other entries?
guided_questions.answer: Every downward step is nondecreasing by the parent rule. No descendant can be smaller than the root.

guided_questions.question: Which parent does an item at index 5 compare with?
guided_questions.answer: Its parent index is (5−1)//2 = 2.

guided_questions.question: Why choose the smaller child during downward repair?
guided_questions.answer: The replacement parent must be no larger than both children. Swapping with the larger child could leave the smaller child above it in priority.

code_examples.title: Use heapq to serve priorities
code_examples.intro: heapify builds the heap. heappop removes its smallest entry.
code_examples.code:
import heapq
jobs = [8, 3, 5, 12, 10]
heapq.heapify(jobs)
print("minimum:", jobs[0])
heapq.heappush(jobs, 4)
served = []
while jobs:
    served.append(heapq.heappop(jobs))
print("served:", served)
code_examples.explanation:
import loads a standard-library module. heapify rearranges the existing list into heap order; it does not return a new sorted list. jobs[0] reads the minimum. heappush adds 4 and repairs the heap.

while jobs repeats until the list is empty. Each heappop returns the current minimum, so the served list is sorted even though the internal heap was not. Heap construction is O(n), each push or pop is O(log n), and removing all items is O(n log n). The output list uses O(n) extra space.
walkthrough: Heapify the five jobs and read the root as the minimum.
Push priority 4 and let heapq restore parent-child order.
Repeatedly remove minima, extending a sorted service history.

code_examples.title: Write the heap insertion repair
code_examples.intro: Watch the new value 4 move from index 5 to index 2.
code_examples.code:
heap = [3, 8, 5, 12, 10]
heap.append(4)
i = len(heap) - 1
swaps = 0
while i > 0:
    parent = (i - 1) // 2
    if heap[parent] <= heap[i]:
        break
    heap[parent], heap[i] = heap[i], heap[parent]
    i = parent
    swaps += 1
print(heap)
print("swaps:", swaps)
print("valid:", all(heap[(j - 1) // 2] <= heap[j] for j in range(1, len(heap))))
code_examples.explanation:
The new value starts at the final index. // finds its parent. The if test stops when the parent already has no larger value. The paired assignment swaps two list entries without losing either. Setting i = parent continues upward from the new position.

Only 4 and 5 swap. all checks that every nonroot item obeys the parent inequality. That final audit scans O(n) entries; it is not part of the O(log n) insertion repair. The repair uses O(1) extra variables. It assumes the original array already satisfied heap order.
walkthrough: Append 4 and initialize i to its new index 5.
Compare with parent index 2 and swap the violating pair.
Stop beneath 3, then independently audit all parent inequalities.

instructor_notes.title: A heap stores just enough order
instructor_notes.body: Priority service needs the next minimum, not a full sorted sequence. Parent-child inequalities guarantee the root is minimal while leaving siblings unordered. If repeated ordered range queries are required, a balanced search tree is often a better match.

instructor_notes.title: Separate repair from the audit
instructor_notes.body: Bubble-up touches only one ancestor route of logarithmic length in a complete tree. The all(...) validation deliberately scans every item. Including that audit after every insertion changes measured total work; it must not be hidden inside an O(log n) claim.

worked_problems.title: Repair one new heap key
worked_problems.question: Append 4 to min-heap [3,8,5,12,10]. Find its final location and count swaps.
worked_problems.strategy: Only the new node’s ancestor path may violate heap order.
steps: The appended value is at index 5; its parent is (5−1)//2=2, holding 5.
Swap 4 and 5. The array becomes [3,8,4,12,10,5].
At index 2, the parent is index 0 holding 3. Since 3≤4, stop.
worked_problems.answer: One swap places 4 at index 2. Every parent is still no larger than its children.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Check all five parent inequalities independently; no sibling ordering is required.

topics.title: Selection, insertion and heap sorting
topics.story:
Amira sorted numbered cards for a school display. At first she searched the whole unsorted pile for the smallest card each time. It worked, but she repeated many comparisons. Then she tried building an ordered row, sliding each new card into place.

The second method was quick when the cards were almost ordered. It was slow when every new card belonged at the beginning. For a large mixed pile, Amira used a heap to keep finding the next extreme. All three methods produced the same order. Their differences appeared in the work needed to maintain that order.
topics.principle:
Sorting puts values into a chosen order. Selection sort finds the smallest remaining value and swaps it into the next position. It makes a quadratic number of comparisons even on sorted input, but only a linear number of swaps.

Insertion sort keeps a sorted prefix. Take the next value, shift larger prefix values right, and place it in the gap. On sorted input, each new value needs little work, so time is Θ(n). Reverse order can require Θ(n²) shifts. Moving only strictly larger values preserves the order of equal-key records. This property is called stability.

Heap sort uses heap order to remove extremes. An in-place ascending version uses a max-heap, sending the largest value to the shrinking right boundary. It gives O(n log n) worst-case time and O(1) extra array storage when repairs are iterative. It is generally not stable. The simple heapq example below instead builds a separate result list, so it does not have that in-place space bound.
topics.formula:
Selection comparisons = (n−1)+(n−2)+⋯+1 = n(n−1)/2
Insertion shifts = number of inversions
Heap sort = O(n log n) worst-case time
topics.symbols:
n is the number of values. Selection compares the first candidate with n−1 others, then n−2, down to 1. The sum is n(n−1)/2.

An inversion is a pair of indices i<j where A[i]>A[j]. The values are in the wrong relative order. Each insertion-sort shift repairs one inversion when the comparison uses strict >. Equal values are not inversions under this rule. The heap-sort cost assumes constant-time comparisons and swaps. Count result lists when reporting an implementation's extra space.
topics.example:
Sort [5,2,4,1] by insertion. Start with sorted prefix [5]. Insert 2 by shifting 5 once, giving [2,5,4,1].

Insert 4 by shifting 5 once, giving [2,4,5,1]. Insert 1 by shifting 5,4 and 2, finishing [1,2,4,5]. There were five shifts, matching the original inversions (5,2),(5,4),(5,1),(2,1),(4,1).

Selection sort instead makes six comparisons across suffixes of lengths four, three and two, regardless of whether the input was already sorted. Heap sort avoids quadratic comparison growth on large arbitrary inputs by maintaining only the heap invariant between removals.
topics.pitfall: Assuming all in-place sorting algorithms are stable, or equating insertion sort’s quadratic worst case with its cost on nearly sorted data.

check.question: Why can insertion sort be useful for small or nearly sorted arrays despite its worst-case bound?
check.answer: Its control overhead is small and work tracks inversions. Few inversions mean few shifts, so the worst-case quadratic pattern may not arise.

glossary.meaning: The beginning of an array that is already in order.
An earlier value that is larger than a later value.
A sort that keeps equal-key records in their original relative order.

guided_questions.question: Why shift right before writing the new value?
guided_questions.answer: The shifts make an empty position while preserving every larger value. Writing first could overwrite a value that is still needed.

guided_questions.question: Why are there five shifts for [5,2,4,1]?
guided_questions.answer: The steps shift 1, then 1, then 3 values. These five shifts match the five original inverted pairs.

guided_questions.question: Is a heapq-based result list an in-place heap sort?
guided_questions.answer: No. It uses another list for the answers. The time can still be O(n log n), but extra storage is O(n).

code_examples.title: Watch insertion sort grow a prefix
code_examples.intro: Print the full array after each insertion and count the values shifted.
code_examples.code:
values = [5, 2, 4, 1]
shifts = 0
for i in range(1, len(values)):
    item = values[i]
    j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and values[j] > item:
        values[j + 1] = values[j]
        j -= 1
        shifts += 1
    values[j + 1] = item
    print(values)
print("shifts:", shifts)
code_examples.explanation:
range begins at 1 because a one-item prefix is already sorted. item saves the next value before shifts overwrite its slot. j walks left. The and test checks the boundary before reading the array. Each larger value moves one position right.

After the loop, j+1 is the correct gap. The prefix through i is now sorted; later positions are still waiting. The printed states show that invariant growing. Worst-case time is O(n²), sorted-input time is O(n), and only a few working variables are added: O(1) extra space.
walkthrough: Save the next unsorted item before shifting any cells.
Move every larger prefix value right until the insertion gap appears.
Write the saved item into the gap and print the enlarged sorted prefix.

code_examples.title: Sort by repeatedly removing a heap minimum
code_examples.intro: This is a clear heap-based sorting version with a separate result list.
code_examples.code:
import heapq
values = [5, 2, 4, 1]
heap = values.copy()
heapq.heapify(heap)
result = []
while heap:
    result.append(heapq.heappop(heap))
print("input:", values)
print("sorted:", result)
code_examples.explanation:
copy preserves the original list. heapify makes the copy a min-heap in O(n) time. Each heappop returns the smallest remaining value, so append extends an already sorted result.

There are n removals, each costing at most O(log n), for O(n log n) total time. The heap copy and result together use O(n) extra space. This program demonstrates the heap-sorting mechanism, not the constant-space max-heap version. It sorts numbers; equal-key records would require an explicit stability policy.
walkthrough: Copy the input so the original remains available for comparison.
Build a min-heap in the copy.
Append each removed minimum to result until the heap is empty.

instructor_notes.title: Use disorder, not only length, to choose a sort
instructor_notes.body: Insertion sort’s shifts equal its inversion count with a strict comparison. A nearly sorted list may have few inversions even when n is fairly large. Selection sort still scans every remaining suffix, so it cannot exploit that same structure.

instructor_notes.title: Stability matters when records have labels
instructor_notes.body: For records with equal score but different arrival times, a stable sort preserves arrival order. Insertion sort must shift only strictly greater keys. Changing > to >= leaves numeric order correct but can reverse equal-key records, violating a stronger contract.

worked_problems.title: Explain five insertion shifts
worked_problems.question: Sort [5,2,4,1] with insertion sort using strict > comparisons. Count shifts and original inversions.
worked_problems.strategy: Each right shift crosses one earlier larger value, so count both ways.
steps: Insert 2: shift 5 once. Insert 4: shift 5 once again.
Insert 1: shift 5,4,2, adding three shifts. Total=1+1+3=5.
Original inversions are (5,2),(5,4),(5,1),(2,1),(4,1): five pairs.
worked_problems.answer: The final array is [1,2,4,5], and the shift count matches the inversion count 5.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Already sorted input has zero inversions and zero shifts, though the outer loop still checks each next item.

topics.title: Hashing, chaining and probing
topics.story:
Leo labeled storage bins with numbers from 0 to 6. He assigned a key to the bin given by its remainder after division by 7. Keys 10, 17 and 24 all wanted bin 3. Leo tried putting them in a small chain there.

He also tested moving along the table until finding an empty slot. That worked until he erased the middle key. Searches stopped at the new gap and missed a later key. Leo replaced the gap with a deleted marker. Searches could now continue. He learned that a fast address rule still needs a careful collision and deletion policy.
topics.principle:
A map connects each key to a value. A hash function turns a key into a bucket number. Different keys can choose the same bucket; this is a collision. Always compare actual keys, not just their hashes. Equal keys must have consistent hashes.

Separate chaining keeps a small collection in each bucket. Its expected lookup cost is O(1+α) under suitable distribution assumptions. The load factor α is stored entries divided by buckets. A poor hash function can still put every key in one bucket, causing O(n) lookup.

Linear probing stores entries directly in table slots. It checks consecutive slots after a collision. A never-used empty slot ends a search. A tombstone marks a deleted slot but does not end the search. Insertion must also handle a full table. Changing table size changes bucket numbers, so resizing needs reinsertion. Expected collision cost and amortized resizing cost are different kinds of average.
topics.formula:
α = n/m
Linear probe j: (h(k)+j) mod m, j=0,1,…
Expected chaining lookup = O(1+α) under uniform hashing assumptions
topics.symbols:
n counts stored entries, and m counts buckets or slots. α=n/m is average entries per bucket. It may exceed 1 for chaining. A probing table needs spare slots, so its operating load should be below 1.

k is a key. h(k) is its initial bucket. j counts how many slots have already been tried. mod wraps h(k)+j into indices 0 through m−1. The expected chaining bound assumes the hash choices spread keys appropriately; load factor alone does not prove it.
topics.example:
Take a seven-slot linear-probing table with h(k)=k mod 7. Insert keys 10,17 and 24. All hash to 3, so they occupy slots 3,4 and 5 respectively.

To find 24, inspect 3, then 4, then 5. Now remove 17. If slot 4 becomes a never-used empty slot, a later search for 24 stops there and incorrectly reports absence.

A tombstone lets that search continue. With separate chaining, the three keys would instead share bucket 3 and be checked in its local container. This example shows that a correct deletion policy is as important as a fast hash computation.
topics.pitfall: Claiming unconditional O(1) hash lookup, or treating a collision as proof that two keys are equal.

check.question: Why does changing table capacity usually require rehashing existing keys?
check.answer: The compression into bucket indices depends on capacity, so old positions may no longer lie on each key’s correct lookup path.

glossary.meaning: A rule that maps a key to a table position.
Two different keys selecting the same initial table position.
A deleted-slot marker that tells a probing search to keep going.

guided_questions.question: Why do 10, 17 and 24 collide modulo 7?
guided_questions.answer: Each leaves remainder 3. A collision is normal and does not mean the keys are equal.

guided_questions.question: Why can search pass a tombstone but stop at None?
guided_questions.answer: Here None means the slot was never occupied. A tombstone means a displaced key may still lie farther along the probe route.

guided_questions.question: Does doubling the number of buckets guarantee constant-time search?
guided_questions.answer: No. Keys could still collide badly. The expected bound also needs suitable hash-distribution assumptions.

code_examples.title: Store colliding keys in one bucket
code_examples.intro: This tiny map uses integer remainders so the printed bucket placement is deterministic.
code_examples.explanation:
The list comprehension creates seven separate empty lists. The underscore means the loop number is unused. key % 7 selects a bucket. append stores a key–value tuple there. lookup scans only that bucket and compares keys.

31 hashes to the same bucket but is absent, so the function returns None. This insert-only demonstration assumes distinct inserted keys; a full map must replace the old value when inserting an existing key. Lookup costs the bucket length: O(n) in the worst case, expected O(1+α) only with suitable hashing.
walkthrough: Create seven independent bucket lists rather than seven references to one list.
Send each integer key to key%7 and preserve its paired value.
Scan bucket 3 using actual key equality for both present 24 and absent 31.

code_examples.title: Delete without breaking a probe chain
code_examples.intro: A unique object marks a deleted slot. It is never printed, so output does not depend on memory addresses.
code_examples.code:
deleted = object()
table = [None] * 7
for key in [10, 17, 24]:
    index = key % 7
    while table[index] is not None:
        index = (index + 1) % 7
    table[index] = key
table[4] = deleted
def contains(key):
    visited = []
    for offset in range(len(table)):
        index = (key % 7 + offset) % 7
        visited.append(index)
        item = table[index]
        if item is None:
            return False, visited
        if item is not deleted and item == key:
            return True, visited
    return False, visited
print(contains(24))
table[4] = None
print(contains(24))
code_examples.explanation:
object() creates a unique marker. The initial inserts place 10, 17 and 24 at slots 3, 4 and 5. Replacing slot 4 with deleted simulates removing 17. contains checks at most the table length, preventing an endless search.

The is not comparison recognizes the marker by identity. The first search passes slot 4 and finds 24. Replacing that marker with None incorrectly ends the second search early. Probing can take O(m) time. The initial insertion loop is deliberately limited to these known nonfull inputs; a complete implementation also needs full-table detection and tombstone reuse.
walkthrough: Insert the three colliding keys in adjacent slots.
Delete 17 with a marker and verify that search for 24 passes it.
Replace the marker with None to demonstrate a broken stopping rule.

instructor_notes.title: An empty slot is a logical certificate
instructor_notes.body: In probing, a never-used empty slot proves the key was never displaced past it under the insertion rule. A deleted slot proves no such thing. A tombstone preserves the route’s history; it is not merely a special visual marker.

instructor_notes.title: Two averages need different arguments
instructor_notes.body: Expected collision cost assumes suitable distribution of hashes. Amortized resizing cost counts copies across updates. A table can have cheap amortized resizing and still suffer linear lookup if every key shares a bucket. See the first chapter’s distinction between expected and amortized cost.

worked_problems.title: Why a tombstone is necessary
worked_problems.question: Insert 10,17,24 into 7 slots using h(k)=k mod 7 and linear probing. Delete 17, then search for 24.
worked_problems.strategy: Follow the exact insertion route and preserve its search stopping rule.
steps: All three keys start at slot 3. They occupy 3,4,5 in that order.
Replace slot 4 by a tombstone. Searching 24 checks 3, passes 4, then succeeds at 5.
If slot 4 were marked never-used, search would stop after two probes and falsely report absence.
worked_problems.answer: A tombstone keeps lookup correct; this successful search uses three slot probes.
worked_problems.sanity_check: A chaining implementation has all three keys in one bucket and can remove 17 without changing other search routes.

topics.title: Cuckoo hashing and collection semantics
topics.story:
Iris organized equipment labels using two small boards. Each label had one allowed spot on each board. When a new label arrived at an occupied spot, Iris moved the old label to its alternative spot. A few moves often made room.

Sometimes moving labels would return to an earlier arrangement. Iris set a move limit and rebuilt the arrangement if that happened. She also noticed that her attendance list needed only membership, while her supply list needed counts. Choosing two storage homes did not decide whether repeated labels should be ignored, replaced or counted. That was a separate rule for the collection.
topics.principle:
Cuckoo hashing gives each key two candidate locations. A lookup checks both locations, so it uses at most two key probes when hash computation and comparison have constant cost. Insertion can evict the current occupant. Move that key to its other location and continue.

A long relocation chain may require new hash functions or a larger table. Thus one insertion is not guaranteed O(1). Expected amortized constant insertion needs suitable random hash families and a sufficiently low load. A move limit prevents infinite loops but does not itself solve the placement problem.

A set records membership. A map stores one value for each key. A multiset records how many times each value occurs. A dictionary of positive counts can implement a multiset. These contracts are separate from the hashing method. Python set, dict and Counter do not promise to use this two-table cuckoo design.
topics.formula:
location(k) ∈ {T₁[h₁(k)], T₂[h₂(k)]}
Multiset total size = Σk count(k)
topics.symbols:
T₁ and T₂ are two arrays. h₁(k) chooses key k's slot in the first array; h₂(k) chooses its slot in the second. The braces list its two permitted homes. Every stored key must occupy one of them.

count(k) is the number of occurrences of k. Σ means sum over distinct keys. The sum gives the total number of occurrences, which can exceed the number of distinct keys. Two-probe lookup counts table positions; expensive key hashing or equality tests need additional work.
topics.example:
Suppose key A occupies its first-table slot 0, with alternative second-table slot 2 free. A new key B also chooses first-table slot 0. Place B there, evict A, then place A in its alternative slot 2.

Both keys now satisfy the two-home invariant, and searching A checks only those two locations. If relocations instead return to an earlier occupied arrangement, rebuild with fresh hash choices rather than loop forever. Separately, inserting red, blue, red into a set yields two distinct members; into a multiset it yields counts red:2 and blue:1, totaling three occurrences.

The collection contract determines which behavior is correct.
topics.pitfall: Transferring cuckoo lookup’s worst-case bound to insertion. An individual insertion can trigger many evictions and a rebuild.

check.question: If a multiset map stores {x:4,y:2}, how many distinct elements and total occurrences are present?
check.answer: Two distinct elements and six occurrences. These are different size measures and should be named explicitly.

glossary.meaning: Replacing a stored key and moving the displaced key to another permitted location.
A collection that remembers whether a value is present, not how many times it was added.
A collection that keeps an occurrence count for each value.

guided_questions.question: Where does key 0 go when key 3 takes its first slot?
guided_questions.answer: Key 0 moves from first[0] to second[0], its other allowed location.

guided_questions.question: Why is a move limit necessary?
guided_questions.answer: A sequence of evictions can cycle. A full implementation must rebuild rather than keep moving forever.

guided_questions.question: How do set and Counter treat red, blue, red?
guided_questions.answer: A set keeps two distinct colors. Counter keeps red:2 and blue:1, for three total occurrences.

code_examples.title: Follow a bounded cuckoo insertion
code_examples.intro: The two hash rules are fixed for this small demonstration. They illustrate relocation, not good general-purpose hashing.
code_examples.code:
first = [None] * 3
second = [None] * 3
def insert(key):
    board = 0
    for _ in range(8):
        table = first if board == 0 else second
        index = key % 3 if board == 0 else (key // 3) % 3
        table[index], key = key, table[index]
        if key is None:
            return
        board = 1 - board
    raise RuntimeError("Rebuild required; an evicted key remains")
for key in [0, 3, 6]:
    insert(key)
print("first:", first)
print("second:", second)
print("3 found:", first[3 % 3] == 3 or second[(3 // 3) % 3] == 3)
code_examples.output:
first: [6, None, None]
second: [0, 3, None]
3 found: True
code_examples.explanation:
board chooses which table to inspect. The paired assignment installs the incoming key and keeps the displaced one in key. If the displaced value is None, the insertion found free space. Otherwise, 1−board switches to its other board.

The final arrangement gives each of 0, 3 and 6 a legal home. Lookup checks only two cells. Insertion can use many moves. The exception signals failure but does not implement rebuilding or rollback; after such a failure a pending key is outside the table. Only the demonstrated successful inputs are a complete insert sequence here.
walkthrough: Try each incoming key in its first-table home.
Keep an evicted key in the local variable and move it to its other table.
Finish only on an empty cell; otherwise signal rebuilding after the move limit.

code_examples.title: Separate membership from multiplicity
code_examples.intro: Use standard-library containers to show what different collection contracts mean.
code_examples.code:
from collections import Counter
colors = ["red", "blue", "red"]
members = set(colors)
counts = Counter(colors)
print("red present:", "red" in members)
print("distinct:", len(members))
print("red count:", counts["red"])
print("total:", sum(counts.values()))
code_examples.output:
red present: True
distinct: 2
red count: 2
total: 3
code_examples.explanation:
set removes duplicate membership entries. Counter builds a mapping from each color to its number of occurrences. The in operator asks about membership; square brackets retrieve a count. values selects the counts, and sum adds them.

The output distinguishes two unique colors from three occurrences. We avoid printing a set because its iteration order is not a stable output format. This code teaches collection semantics, not cuckoo internals. Counting the n inputs takes expected O(n) work under normal hash-table assumptions and O(k) space for k distinct colors.
walkthrough: Use the same three color occurrences for both containers.
Ask set for membership and Counter for the number of red occurrences.
Compare distinct count with the sum of all occurrence counts.

instructor_notes.title: A failed insertion must not lose a key
instructor_notes.body: During eviction, one key is held outside the tables in the local variable. If the move limit is reached, rebuilding must include that pending key as well as stored keys. Throwing an exception alone is only a demonstration boundary, not a complete recoverable map update.

instructor_notes.title: Collection meaning precedes storage
instructor_notes.body: A map replaces one value for a repeated key; a set ignores repeated membership; a multiset increments a count. Two-probe cuckoo lookup does not decide among these contracts. Specify the desired result before selecting the implementation.

worked_problems.title: Trace the displaced key
worked_problems.question: Two tables each have three slots. h₁(k)=k mod 3, h₂(k)=floor(k/3) mod 3. Insert 0,3,6 by trying table 1 first.
worked_problems.strategy: Track the incoming key separately from keys already occupying legal homes.
steps: 0 enters first[0]. Inserting 3 replaces it there and sends 0 to second[0].
Inserting 6 replaces 3 at first[0]. Key 3 moves to second[1].
The legal homes are now first[0]=6, second[0]=0, second[1]=3.
worked_problems.answer: All three keys are stored. Lookup for 3 checks first[0] then second[1], at most two probes.
worked_problems.sanity_check: Check both hash formulas for every stored key. This successful trace does not bound every possible insertion chain.

topics.title: Graphs and representation choices
topics.story:
Nia drew a map of five rooms. A line represented a corridor. Four rooms formed a loop, and the fifth room had no corridor. She counted five rooms and four lines and initially called the map a tree.
